title: Cultural Awareness in Global AI | Cohere
gist: Cohere's analysis of 5.6 million training samples finds a 'culture funnel': cultural signals present in pretraining data shrink sharply through SFT, alignment, and reasoning stages, and adding explicit cultural markers during fine-tuning (rather than more raw cultural data) recovers cultural benchmark performance without hurting general capability.

themes.theme: The culture funnel in LLM training pipelines

insights.claim: Analyzing over 5.6 million training samples across pretraining, SFT, alignment, and reasoning stages, Cohere found that cultural diversity in the data narrows consistently as it moves from pretraining into post-training, a pattern they term the 'culture funnel'.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: Industry-standard post-training pipelines (SFT/alignment/RLHF-style stages) may be systematically stripping cultural nuance out of models regardless of how culturally rich the pretraining corpus was, a hidden quality gap for any AI vendor competing on global/localized deployment.
insights.quote: we found a consistent pattern: cultural diversity narrows as data moves from pretraining into post-training. We call this phenomenon the culture funnel.
insights.locator: Finding 1: Cultural signals get lost in post-training data

insights.claim: Post-training datasets used to improve reasoning and alignment are disproportionately weighted toward technical tasks like math and code, which contain few cultural markers, crowding out culturally grounded content from the data models are fine-tuned on.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: The current wave of reasoning/math/code-heavy fine-tuning data (used broadly across the industry) is a structural cause of cultural blind spots, not just a labeling gap - implies a tradeoff between reasoning-benchmark gains and cultural competence unless data curation is deliberately rebalanced.
insights.locator: Finding 1: Cultural signals get lost in post-training data

insights.claim: Because remaining cultural content is concentrated in fact-based categories like food, holidays, and named entities, models trained on it tend to do well on trivia-style cultural benchmarks but struggle at reasoning about implicit cultural norms, preferences, and social dynamics.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: Benchmark scores on 'cultural' fact-recall tests can overstate a model's real-world cultural competence, a gap investors and enterprise buyers evaluating AI vendors on 'global readiness' claims should probe rather than take at face value.
insights.locator: Finding 1: Cultural signals get lost in post-training data

themes.theme: Multilingual scale does not equal cultural coverage

insights.claim: As more languages are added to a training dataset, geographic diversity keeps increasing but the overall proportion of culturally grounded content plateaus, meaning multilingual scaling has diminishing returns for actual cultural representation.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: Challenges the common go-to-market claim that adding language support equals cultural/global readiness; investors should treat 'N languages supported' as a weak proxy for genuine cultural alignment in AI products.
insights.quote: expanding multilingual coverage has diminishing returns in increasing the overall percentage of culturally grounded data in pretraining and SFT datasets
insights.locator: Finding 2: More languages means more geographic diversity but not more culture

insights.claim: The Aya dataset carries a much higher proportion of cultural content than comparable datasets specifically because it was built through intentional curation from an international community of contributors, not because it covers more languages.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: Demonstrates a replicable lever - community-sourced, intentionally curated data - that outperforms raw language-count scaling for cultural representation, relevant to how AI labs should prioritize data-sourcing spend.
insights.quote: the Aya dataset has a much higher proportion of cultural content, because it intentionally curated culturally-grounded prompts and responses from an international community of contributors
insights.locator: Finding 2: More languages means more geographic diversity but not more culture

themes.theme: Geographic skew in cultural training data

insights.claim: Within culturally tagged training data, India is the most frequently represented geolocation, alongside a concentration of Asian and European countries, while South America, Africa, and North America outside the US each contribute only about one country to the top 50 geolocations in datasets like CulturaX.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: Even language-fluent global AI products will systematically underserve users in Africa, South America, and much of North America because their cultural context is barely present in training data, an underappreciated localization/product risk for AI companies expanding into emerging markets.
insights.quote: only a single South American, one African, and one North American country appear within the top 50 geolocations
insights.locator: Finding 3: Geographic Representation is Heavily Skewed in Cultural Data

insights.claim: Besides India, China and the USA are the other dominant geolocations ranking in the top 10 across most datasets studied, and cultural knowledge tied to underrepresented regions remains hard for models to learn even when the local language itself is well represented in training data.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: Confirms a long-tail concentration risk (India/China/US dominance) in the data underlying most current LLMs, a structural bias investors should factor into assessments of AI cultural/regional bias claims and regulatory scrutiny.
insights.locator: Finding 3: Geographic Representation is Heavily Skewed in Cultural Data

themes.theme: Where cultural awareness actually matters in use

insights.claim: Translation, local information requests, and message writing carry the strongest cultural signals in training data, while coding and medical tasks carry the fewest explicit cultural markers, yet a user survey found people most want better cultural awareness in creative writing, translation, and email/message writing, closely matching where training data does carry cultural signal.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: Gives AI product teams a task-level roadmap for where to prioritize cultural-alignment investment first (translation, messaging, creative writing) versus where current gaps are largest relative to unmet user need (medical, business contexts).

insights.claim: Users report needing cultural awareness across a wider range of tasks - including medical and business contexts - than current training data distributions reflect, indicating an unmet-need gap beyond what training data curation currently addresses.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: Signals a growth area for enterprise AI (medical, business/legal) where cultural-context features are underbuilt relative to demand, a potential differentiation opportunity for vendors willing to curate domain-specific cultural data.

themes.theme: Fixing the funnel with explicit cultural markers

insights.claim: Cohere fine-tuned its TinyAya base model by adding explicit cultural markers as metadata to training samples, without changing the underlying data distribution, and saw gains of +8% on NormAd, +6% on BBQ, and +2.3% on GMMLU versus baseline, without sacrificing general multilingual capability.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: A concrete, low-cost technique (metadata tagging rather than data collection) that materially improves cultural benchmark performance - a reproducible method other AI labs could adopt cheaply to close cultural gaps.
insights.quote: gains of +8% on NormAd, +6% on BBQ, and +2.3% on GMMLU

insights.claim: Training on 'more cultural' data without explicit markers produces smaller cultural-benchmark gains than the marker-based approach and also degrades general model capabilities, whereas explicit tagging avoids that tradeoff.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: Runs counter to the intuitive fix of simply sourcing more culturally-themed data; investors evaluating AI data-curation vendors should look for metadata/tagging methodology, not just claimed dataset volume or diversity.

insights.claim: Cohere argues that data pipelines themselves function as alignment mechanisms, meaning the composition choices made at each training stage - not just explicit alignment techniques - determine which cultural knowledge remains learnable by a model.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: Reframes 'alignment' as a data-engineering problem rather than purely a post-hoc RLHF/prompting problem; AI companies claiming cultural or value alignment should be evaluated on data pipeline design, not just alignment-stage tuning.
insights.quote: data pipelines themselves act as alignment mechanisms, shaping which kinds of cultural knowledge remain learnable by models

insights.claim: Cohere predicts that genuine cultural capability in future LLMs will not emerge automatically from scaling data volume, but will require intentionally designed data pipelines that balance representation across languages, geolocations, domains, and task intents.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: Positions deliberate multi-dimensional data curation (not raw scale) as the differentiator for 'globally aware' AI products, a thesis investors can use to evaluate which labs are investing in this versus relying on scale alone.

insights.claim: To generate its cultural signal tags at scale, Cohere used its own Command A model to automatically tag prompts, validating tag quality via manual review of a subset across six languages.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: Shows Cohere using its flagship Command A model as an internal research/data-curation tool, an example of a lab applying its own model to improve its own training pipeline - a data point on internal model utility beyond customer-facing use.
insights.locator: Looking for culture along the training pipeline
